doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Starting a jazz string group and writing for strings
summary: He formed a ten-piece string group to teach jazz phrasing, writes the charts himself, and cites Calvin Custer, Alan Broadbent and Claus Ogerman.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Absolutely. And I won’t do that. And one of the reasons I started a string group was I want the string players — for that small percentage who do get picked up by major orchestras and are earning a paycheck with a major orchestra — to be able to interpret the oddities of jazz phrasing, and to have another paycheck from the other side of the street, and so I’m teaching people how to phrase running eighth notes with the underlying 12/8 feel, and the oddities of chordal placement, and the chord voicings, so that the clashes don’t become foreign or frightening to them. Because a lot of things people are doing for strings, and I work a lot with the Buffalo Philharmonic, major acts will come in and the string parts are dumbed down so hard, whereas they can do some beautiful stuff, things that John Williams has written, or Alan Broadbent has written, things which have a bit of a technical challenge, which creates interest within the string section. And once you have a bunch of people interested in backing up the front person you really get that support. And I started the strings kind of as a selfish move. Because I’ve always loved playing with strings. And nobody was doing it. Nobody was playing jazz with strings. And the only things that I found out the publishers have is in a Beatles medley for beginners strings, and this is stuff that their grandparents listened to. They’re not familiar with The Beatles, at all. They listen to a whole other bunch of things. So I’m trying to bring some different things so that we do some good standards, we do some ballads, we do some Brazilian things, and some kind of soft rock/pop things.
And how many do you have?

Ten. Ten strings. And I use first, second, third violins, like Charlie Parker’s stuff. And nowadays it’s usually first and second and then violas. But I have two firsts, two seconds, two thirds, two violas, two cellos. And then piano, bass, drums, guitar — and I’ll send you a track of a beautiful Vienna singer — and I don’t play on it but I wrote a viola solo © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -19-

for this kid. Because you don’t hear viola solos too often. And he was thrilled to come up front. He played it, and the applause was deafening and he had this big smile on his face. They relax on stage when they’re playing this stuff with me. I kind of take a glance on the cello — they’re grooving — and it’s really delightful.
And you’re writing with a pencil and paper.

Yes. And I’m having to do it all because there’s nothing out there that’s been published. There’s a great writer by the name of Calvin Custer who is the Syracuse Symphony’s musical director. I have a couple of his things. And when I first started writing, that was the model that was taken. Him, Alan Broadbent, Claus Ogerman. And he was using three violins as well. And the sound that he got, and the strength that he got, it was just a huge, big, warm layer of sound, which was just so nice.
